item.title: Letters from the Stage: What Singers Wish Conductors and Theater Managers Knew
item.description: An open letter addressing the hidden challenges opera singers face in rehearsal rooms worldwide. Seven practical insights on vocal health, emotional safety, audition feedback, and creating collaborative environments where artists can take risks. Essential reading for conductors, directors, and theater administrators who want to understand what singers truly need to deliver their best performances.
item.content:encoded:
Dear Maestros, Intendants, and Artistic Administrators,

We love you. We really do. We know how much you juggle—budgets, schedules, egos, crises. We know you're doing your best under impossible constraints. But from our place under the lights, there are some things we deeply wish you understood. Not to accuse, not to criticize—but to help us all make better art, together.

Because if you listen carefully, the voice onstage might be telling you more than just the score.

1. Our Instrument Is Our Body—And It's Always in Flux

Unlike a violinist or flutist, we can't replace strings or polish valves. Singers carry our instruments in our ribs, throat, lungs, and nervous system. That means we walk into rehearsal with the same body that slept poorly, fought a cold, or held its breath after a tense phone call...

item.title: From Shul to Stage: Breathing Together in Chazzanut and Opera
item.description: How cantorial prayer and operatic performance share the same breath, technique, and spiritual foundation. From Thomas Heyer's teachings on voice as 'vessel of the soul' to leading Yom Kippur services and singing Mozart, discover why sacred and secular music traditions strengthen each other rather than compete—and how physiological empathy connects performer and audience through shared breathing.
item.content:encoded:
When people discover that I'm both a chazzan (cantor) and an opera singer, their first question is often, "Do those two worlds ever get mixed up?" The answer is yes—but not in the way they expect. The disciplines of chazzanut and classical singing don't merely coexist for me. They are in constant, vibrant conversation.

The Voice as Vessel of Soul

One of the most formative ideas I encountered as a voice student came from Prof. Thomas Heyer, my second voice teacher during university. He loved to (intentionally) mis-translate the word person from Latin per sonare: "to sound through." While not linguistically accurate, the idea behind it was profound. To him, and eventually to me, the voice is the vessel of the soul.

item.title: Becoming Wagner's Alberich: The Challenge of Power and Restraint
item.description: Preparing Wagner's cunning Nibelung dwarf at Harztheater revealed unexpected vocal and dramatic challenges. From mastering the Coburger Fassung's reduced orchestration to embodying psychological complexity on stage, Alberich demands far more than Wagnerian power—it requires technical precision, emotional vulnerability, and the courage to find humanity in opera's most demanding villain roles.
item.content:encoded:
Preparing for the role of Alberich in Richard Wagner's Das Rheingold has been one of the most demanding and transformative experiences of my operatic career. Alberich is a character steeped in complexity—a villain driven by rage, rejection, and ambition. Portraying this iconic figure requires far more than vocal power; it demands a deep psychological understanding, physical adaptability, and a finely tuned vocal technique capable of both explosive force and subtle restraint.

The Vocal Landscape of Alberich

Wagner's writing for Alberich sits in the challenging range of a bass-baritone, calling for immense vocal stamina paired with agility. Unlike some Wagnerian roles that rely on sheer volume, Alberich's character thrives in nuanced expression...
